Figure 12. Left: the 3,000 frames on the first two principal components of the C-alpha coordinates (46.5 % and 21.3 % of the variance), coloured by run — the six runs occupy largely separate regions. Centre: the same projection coloured by the K = 4 clusters, which reproduce the run structure. Right: cluster index against time; A1, A2 and A3 each stay in one cluster for the whole nanosecond, and only B2 and B3 switch.

The table quantifies what the figure shows, and it is the key result: at \(K=4\) the adjusted Rand index against run identity is 0.503, against temperature 0.058. The clusters are not metastable states of Trp-cage; they are the six trajectories. Each run relaxed from the same minimised structure into its own corner of shape space and stayed there (replica A3 at 0.251 nm mean RMSD, A1 at 0.110 nm, the rest between), so a frame’s cluster says which simulation it came from. The cross-tabulation is worth reading row by row: cluster 3 is essentially A1 plus B1, cluster 4 is all of A3, and only B2 and B3 are split between clusters.

Domain context — why 1 ns is not enough, and what this costs

Trp-cage folds and unfolds on a timescale of microseconds; its experimental melting temperature is about 315 K. In 1 ns at 340 K the molecule has had time to jiggle, not to unfold. Worse, the frames within one run are strongly autocorrelated, so a 1 ns run contains only a handful of statistically independent samples even though it contributes 500 rows to the table. Clustering treats every row as an independent object, which is why a per-frame clustering of a short ensemble recovers the replica structure: the between-replica differences are real and large, and the within-replica variation is small and correlated. The honest sentence for a paper based on data like these is: “frames cluster by replica rather than by conformational state, indicating that 1 ns per replica does not sample the relevant transitions”.

The machinery is still useful: the medoid frames above are genuine structures (not averages, which are geometrically distorted), annotated with run and time stamp, and each cluster’s mean RMSD to its own centroid — 0.057 to 0.088 nm — quantifies how tight the “state” is. That is the deliverable a structural project wants, provided the caption says “representative frame of cluster k” and not “conformational state k”.

11. The lab’s fourth task: are there patient subgroups?

The expression slice holds 138 biopsies: one diseased and one healthy gingival site from each of 69 patients[27]. The clinical question is whether the tissues fall into molecular subtypes — a claim made for this cohort[26]; the methodological question is what a clustering of 138 samples by 1,000 genes can support. Here we have an external label (clinical status), so every partition can be scored with the ARI rather than admired. Genes are z-scored so that highly expressed genes do not dominate, and correlation distance (profile shape) is compared with Euclidean distance on z-scores.

v   <- apply(E, 1, var); sel <- order(v, decreasing = TRUE)[1:1000]
sub_expr <- E[sel, ]; samples <- colnames(sub_expr)
status <- as.integer(meta$status[match(samples, meta$sample_id)] == "diseased")
Zg <- scale(t(sub_expr))                                   # samples x genes, gene-wise z-scores
Dcorr <- as.dist(1 - cor(sub_expr))                        # correlation distance between samples
cat(sprintf("1,000 most variable genes x %d samples; selected-gene variance %.2f to %.2f\n",
            ncol(sub_expr), min(v[sel]), max(v)))
## 1,000 most variable genes x 138 samples; selected-gene variance 0.51 to 14.59
cat(sprintf("correlation distance between samples: min %.3f, median %.3f, max %.3f\n",
            min(Dcorr), median(Dcorr), max(Dcorr)))
## correlation distance between samples: min 0.004, median 0.198, max 0.826
results <- list()
for (meth in c("average", "complete", "ward.D2"))
  results[[paste0("correlation + ", meth)]] <- cutree(hclust(Dcorr, method = meth), 2)
results[["euclidean(z) + ward"]] <- cutree(hclust(dist(Zg), method = "ward.D2"), 2)
set.seed(0); results[["k-means on z-scores"]] <- kmeans(Zg, 2, nstart = 10)$cluster
pcg <- prcomp(Zg, center = FALSE)
set.seed(0); results[["k-means on 5 PCs"]] <- kmeans(pcg$x[, 1:5], 2, nstart = 10)$cluster
for (nm in names(results))
  cat(sprintf("%-22s sizes %-7s ARI vs diseased/healthy %.3f\n", nm,
              paste(table(results[[nm]]), collapse = "/"), ari(status, results[[nm]])))
## correlation + average  sizes 137/1   ARI vs diseased/healthy 0.000
## correlation + complete sizes 137/1   ARI vs diseased/healthy 0.000
## correlation + ward.D2  sizes 73/65   ARI vs diseased/healthy 0.384
## euclidean(z) + ward    sizes 89/49   ARI vs diseased/healthy 0.315
## k-means on z-scores    sizes 68/70   ARI vs diseased/healthy 0.440
## k-means on 5 PCs       sizes 68/70   ARI vs diseased/healthy 0.440
evg <- pcg$sdev^2/sum(pcg$sdev^2)
pdat <- data.frame(PC1 = pcg$x[, 1], PC2 = pcg$x[, 2],
                   status = factor(status, 0:1, c("healthy", "diseased")))
g1 <- ggplot(pdat, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = status)) + geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = .85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")])) +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f%%)", 100*evg[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f%%)", 100*evg[2]),
       title = "Samples in PC space") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
print(g1)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))
for (meth in c("average", "ward.D2")) {
  hc <- hclust(Dcorr, method = meth)
  plot(hc, labels = FALSE, hang = -1, xlab = "", sub = "", ylab = "merge height",
       main = sprintf("correlation + %s\nARI = %.2f", meth, ari(status, cutree(hc, 2))), cex.main = .95)
  points(seq_along(hc$order), rep(par("usr")[3], length(hc$order)),
         col = ifelse(status[hc$order] == 1, PAL["orange"], PAL["blue"]), pch = 15, cex = .5, xpd = NA)
}

par(op)

Figure 13. Top: the 138 biopsies on their first two principal components; diseased (orange) and healthy (blue) sites separate along PC1, which carries 34 % of the variance. Bottom: dendrograms from the same correlation-distance matrix under average and Ward linkage, with each leaf’s clinical status drawn underneath. Average linkage chains — its two-cluster cut isolates one outlying sample and leaves the other 137 together (ARI 0.000) — while Ward splits the cohort 73/65 in line with disease status (ARI 0.384).

Two methodological conclusions and one biological caution.

  • The linkage, not the distance, decided the answer. All three correlation-based clusterings used an identical matrix; average and complete linkage both returned a 137/1 split with ARI exactly 0.000, and only Ward recovered the clinical signal. A hierarchical clustering reported without its linkage is not reproducible.
  • An ARI of 0.38 to 0.44 against a two-class label is moderate agreement, not a discovery. The dominant axis of variation in gingival tissue is inflammation, so unsupervised clustering rediscovers the label it was not given. Plain k-means on the z-scores (0.440) beat every hierarchical variant, the opposite of what the dendrogram’s visual authority suggests.
  • Subtype claims must respect the paired design. Each patient contributed two samples, so the 138 rows are not 138 independent observations.

12. The clusters that are not there

The final hazard is visual. Non-linear embeddings — t-SNE[24][35] and UMAP — optimise a neighbourhood-preserving 2-D layout, and will produce visible groups whether or not the data contains any, because the optimisation pushes apart points that are not near neighbours. Distances between blobs, their sizes and even their number (which depends on perplexity) are not interpretable[24]; the single-cell genomics literature has been through a public reckoning on this point[25].

The experiment: take 400 points of pure 50-dimensional Gaussian noise — a data set with, by construction, exactly one cluster — embed it with Rtsne at three perplexities, run k-means on the embedding, and compute the silhouette of the resulting partition twice: in the embedding, and in the original data.

set.seed(1); Xnoise <- matrix(rnorm(400*50), 400, 50)
Dnoise <- dist(Xnoise); noise_emb <- list()
nrows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(5, 30, 100), function(perp) {
  set.seed(0)
  e <- Rtsne(Xnoise, dims = 2, perplexity = perp, pca = TRUE,
             check_duplicates = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)$Y
  set.seed(0); lab <- kmeans(e, 4, nstart = 10)$cluster
  noise_emb[[as.character(perp)]] <<- data.frame(x = e[, 1], y = e[, 2], g = factor(lab), perp = perp)
  data.frame(perplexity = perp,
             silhouette_in_embedding = mean(silhouette(lab, dist(e))[, 3]),
             silhouette_of_same_labels_in_data = mean(silhouette(lab, Dnoise)[, 3])) }))
knitr::kable(nrows, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Four k-means clusters imposed on t-SNE maps of pure noise")
Four k-means clusters imposed on t-SNE maps of pure noise
perplexity silhouette_in_embedding silhouette_of_same_labels_in_data
5 0.349 0.000
30 0.333 0.007
100 0.334 0.015 
cat("The data is isotropic Gaussian noise: the true number of clusters is 1.\n")
## The data is isotropic Gaussian noise: the true number of clusters is 1.
nd_all <- do.call(rbind, noise_emb)
nd_all$lab <- factor(sprintf("perplexity %d (silhouette %.2f in map, %.2f in data)", nd_all$perp,
  nrows$silhouette_in_embedding[match(nd_all$perp, nrows$perplexity)],
  nrows$silhouette_of_same_labels_in_data[match(nd_all$perp, nrows$perplexity)]))
print(ggplot(nd_all, aes(x, y, colour = g)) + geom_point(size = .7, show.legend = FALSE) +
        facet_wrap(~ lab, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
        scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL)) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
        theme(axis.text = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(size = 7)))

Figure 14. t-SNE maps of 400 points of 50-dimensional Gaussian noise at three perplexities, coloured by k-means run on the map itself. Every panel shows apparent islands with a silhouette in the map of 0.33 to 0.35 — the range a referee accepts as “well separated” — while the same labels score between 0.000 and 0.015 in the original data.

The rule that follows is simple and worth memorising.

Cluster in the data space; use the embedding only to display the clustering. Never cluster on t-SNE or UMAP coordinates, and never count blobs in a map.

The correct practice is below: a t-SNE of the 2,764 compounds, computed from 50 truncated-SVD components of the sparse bit matrix (irlba, which never densifies it), coloured by the Butina clusters obtained from the full-dimensional Tanimoto distances.

t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
set.seed(0); sv <- irlba(FP, nv = 50)
P <- as.matrix(FP %*% sv$v)
set.seed(0); emb <- Rtsne(P, dims = 2, perplexity = 30, pca = FALSE,
                          check_duplicates = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)$Y
cat(sprintf("SVD + t-SNE of %d compounds in %.1f s\n", nrow(P), proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0))
## SVD + t-SNE of 2764 compounds in 4.5 s
topc <- as.integer(names(sort(table(lab_butina), decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]))
cat("six largest Butina clusters (id:size):",
    paste(topc, table(lab_butina)[as.character(topc)], sep = ":", collapse = "  "), "\n")
## six largest Butina clusters (id:size): 1:96  2:56  3:42  5:41  7:35  6:33
set.seed(0); ss <- sample(nrow(P), 1500)
cat(sprintf("silhouette of the Butina partition in the t-SNE map: %.3f; in the Tanimoto space it was computed on: %.3f\n",
            mean(silhouette(lab_butina[ss], dist(emb[ss, ]))[, 3]),
            mean(silhouette(lab_butina[ss], as.dist(D[ss, ss]))[, 3])))
## silhouette of the Butina partition in the t-SNE map: 0.018; in the Tanimoto space it was computed on: 0.132
ed <- data.frame(x = emb[, 1], y = emb[, 2], pAct = cmp$pActivity,
                 series = ifelse(lab_butina %in% topc, as.character(lab_butina), NA))
g1 <- ggplot(ed, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(colour = "grey82", size = .4) +
  geom_point(data = subset(ed, !is.na(series)), aes(colour = series), size = .9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(unname(PAL), "#8c8c3a", "#a3324f")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Butina clusters shown on a t-SNE map") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
g2 <- ggplot(ed, aes(x, y, colour = pAct)) + geom_point(size = .4) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "pActivity") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "The same map coloured by potency") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
print(g1 | g2)

Figure 15. Left: the collection embedded with t-SNE from 50 SVD components of the fingerprints; grey points are all compounds, colours mark the six largest Butina clusters (96, 56, 42, 41, 35 and 33 compounds), and each series lands in a compact island — a visual check that the clustering computed in the full space is coherent. Right: the identical layout coloured by potency, which varies within every island.

Two numbers above are the inverse of the noise experiment: the Butina partition scores 0.132 in the Tanimoto space where it was computed and only 0.018 in the map, because t-SNE spends its degrees of freedom on local neighbourhoods and 961 small clusters cannot all be separated in two dimensions. A silhouette computed in an embedding is therefore uninformative in both directions: high for structure that does not exist, low for structure that does.

Domain context — what “a cluster of actives” does and does not imply

A compact island of highly potent compounds is usually a publication artefact before it is a biological fact: one group published a series, optimised it to nanomolar potency and deposited forty analogues, so the cluster records the history of the field rather than a privileged region of chemical space. The 96-compound series of Section 8, median pActivity 7.61 against 6.44 for the table, is such a record — the bias that makes random splits optimistic.

Bridge

Similarity and fingerprints are developed from chemistry first principles in the cheminformatics course, units U5 (descriptors and fingerprints), U8 (chemical space) and U11 (similarity and SAR); read U5 if the word “fingerprint” is new. The simulation that produced the Trp-cage frames is explained in the bioinformatics course, BGM324 unit 05 (molecular dynamics), and the structural-biology vocabulary in unit 02. The artificial-intelligence course covers unsupervised learning from the algorithms’ side: BGM411 study material (R edition). Inside this course the natural continuations are Unit 16 (interpretability), which asks what a supervised model learned, and Unit 17 (uncertainty and applicability domain), which is a distance question again; the deep-learning view of learned representations is Unit 18. The Python edition of this unit, with RDKit’s own Butina implementation and molecule drawings, is here. 

summary_tab <- data.frame(
  data = c("ROCK1 descriptors (11-D, z-scored)", "ROCK1 descriptors", "ROCK1 descriptors",
           "ROCK1 fingerprints (Tanimoto)", "ROCK1 fingerprints", "MD frames (C-alpha RMSD)",
           "138 biopsies (correlation)", "400 points of pure noise"),
  method = c(sprintf("k-means, K chosen by silhouette (K = %d)", best_sil),
             sprintf("DBSCAN by hand, eps = %.1f", dbrows$eps[3]),
             sprintf("diagonal GMM, BIC-selected (K = %d)", bst$K),
             sprintf("Butina t = 0.35 (%d clusters)", K_but),
             sprintf("average linkage, same K (%d)", K_but),
             "k-means, K = 4", "Ward linkage, cut at 2", "k-means on a t-SNE map"),
  quality = c(sprintf("silhouette %.3f", max(swp$silhouette)),
              sprintf("%.0f%% noise, %d clusters", dbrows$noise_pct[3], dbrows$clusters[3]),
              sprintf("%.0f%% ambiguous (max resp < 0.8)", 100*mean(mx < 0.8)),
              sprintf("ARI vs scaffold %.2f", ari(lab_scaf, lab_butina)),
              sprintf("ARI vs Butina %.2f", ari(lab_butina, lab_agg)),
              sprintf("ARI vs run %.2f / vs temperature %.2f", ari(run_of_frame, lab_md),
                      ari(cond_of_frame, lab_md)),
              sprintf("ARI vs status %.2f", ari(status, results[["correlation + ward.D2"]])),
              sprintf("silhouette %.2f in map vs %.2f in data",
                      nrows$silhouette_in_embedding[2], nrows$silhouette_of_same_labels_in_data[2])),
  verdict = c("a continuum, not groups", "no density scale", "BIC keeps falling", "usable series",

ROCK1 descriptors diagonal GMM, BIC-selected (K = 8) 3% ambiguous (max resp < 0.8) BIC keeps falling
ROCK1 fingerprints (Tanimoto) Butina t = 0.35 (961 clusters) ARI vs scaffold 0.28 usable series
ROCK1 fingerprints average linkage, same K (961) ARI vs Butina 0.60 same distances, different answer
MD frames (C-alpha RMSD) k-means, K = 4 ARI vs run 0.50 / vs temperature 0.06 clusters = replicas
138 biopsies (correlation) Ward linkage, cut at 2 ARI vs status 0.38 recovers the known label
400 points of pure noise k-means on a t-SNE map silhouette 0.33 in map vs 0.01 in data entirely artefactual

Table 1. Every partition computed in this unit, with the measurement that decided whether to believe it. Three of the eight rows are negative results.

13. Summary

Clustering cannot fail loudly: it always returns labels, and the labels always look like a finding, so the discipline has to come from the analyst. This unit built that discipline in five layers.

The metric is the model. Euclidean distance on standardised descriptors, Tanimoto on fingerprints[19], RMSD on superposed conformations and correlation on expression profiles answer four different questions about closeness. The Tanimoto matrix of 2,764 compounds is three lines of Matrix algebra and under a second; the same matrix for a 100,000-compound catalogue would be 40 GB, so the algorithm must be chosen to avoid building it.

Five algorithm families, each with its geometry. k-means assumes spherical, equal-spread, equal-size clusters and failed visibly on sheared (ARI 0.48), unequal-variance (0.58), unequal-size (0.32) and non-convex (0.21) data. Agglomerative clustering returns the whole family of partitions, and the linkage is a strong assumption: on an identical matrix, average linkage isolated a single outlier from 138 biopsies while Ward recovered the clinical label. Density methods need no \(K\) and allow noise, but a single \(\varepsilon\) cannot serve several densities, and HDBSCAN[11], which solves this, is the one algorithm of the unit this environment could not run. Gaussian mixtures add soft assignments and BIC[14]; a hand-written EM showed BIC falling monotonically to the largest K tried, which means the density is not a mixture of a few separated Gaussians. Butina’s leader algorithm[18] is the chemistry-specific tool: one pass, a real molecule at each centre, one interpretable cutoff.

Validity is three measurements, not one. Internal indices (silhouette[3], Davies-Bouldin[4], Calinski-Harabasz[5]) presuppose convex clusters; external indices (ARI[15]) need a label and have a verified zero at chance; stability[17] refutes a partition but cannot confirm it, as the high stability of a low-silhouette partition showed. The elbow is not evidence — uniform noise produced the same bend, and only the gap statistic[6] reported “no structure” correctly.

The four lab tasks, honestly reported. Series detection gives a usable partition — 961 clusters at \(t=0.35\), the largest holding 96 compounds across 17 formal scaffolds — provided you do not confuse clusters with scaffolds[20]. Diversity picking can be proved to work against random selection (8.4 standard deviations, p < 0.005 with 200 draws), and the minimum pairwise distance is the statistic that matters. Conformational clustering of a 1 ns replica ensemble recovers the replicas (ARI 0.50 against run, 0.06 against temperature), a result about sampling rather than about the protein. Patient clustering recovers the clinical label it was not given: a sanity check, not a subtype discovery.

The visual trap. t-SNE will show islands in pure noise: the silhouette computed in the map was about 0.34 against 0.01 for the same labels in the data[24][25]. The converse also holds — a real Butina partition scored 0.132 in Tanimoto space and 0.018 in the map. Cluster in the data space, colour the map.

Everything here is computed from the public ROCK1 table[28] in base R[30] with data.table, the tidyverse[31] through ggplot2[32], cluster[33], Matrix and Rtsne; dendextend[34] colours dendrograms beyond what the base plot offers. What none of them provides is the decision about whether the answer means anything.

14. Self-assessment

  1. Why can inertia never be used to choose K, and what does the gap statistic add?

Inertia is the objective k-means minimises, and adding a centroid can only reduce it; the curve is monotone decreasing by construction, reaching zero when K = n. The gap statistic compares the observed log inertia with the log inertia of uniform reference data in the same bounding box, so it measures how much more structure the data has than a structureless null. In Section 7 the gap stayed within one standard error of zero for uniform noise — correctly reporting “no clusters” where the elbow of the same data suggested K = 3.

  1. A colleague clusters 2,000 compounds with k-means on raw 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints and reports the centroid of each cluster as “the representative compound of the series”. Give two distinct objections.

First, a centroid of binary vectors is a vector of fractions: it corresponds to no molecule and cannot be drawn, synthesised or docked, whereas a leader or medoid method returns a real compound. Second, squared Euclidean distance on sparse binary data is dominated by bits zero in both molecules — 1,967 of 2,048 for the pair in Section 2.1.

  1. Single and average linkage on the same Tanimoto matrix give different partitions. Is one of them wrong?

Neither is wrong; they encode different definitions of “close sets”. Where almost all pairwise distances are large, both tend to chain, so a cut yields one giant cluster plus singletons — a correct execution of the rule and an unusable partition. Section 4 showed both returning a cluster of ~590 of 600 compounds at K = 4 while Ward returned four balanced groups. Choose the linkage before looking at results, and remember that in R ward.D2, not ward.D, implements Ward’s criterion on distances.

  1. What does a mean silhouette of 0.29 tell you, and what does it hide?

It says that on average a point is only slightly closer to its own cluster than to the nearest other cluster — a weak partition. It hides the distribution: Figure 8 showed 10–21 % of compounds with negative silhouettes (points closer to a neighbouring cluster than to their own) and at least one cluster whose mean is near zero. Always plot the per-point silhouettes.

  1. Your clustering of 138 biopsies is highly stable under 80 % resampling. Can you conclude the subgroups are real?

No. Stability is necessary but not sufficient: a reproducible way of cutting a single elongated cloud in half is stable because the cloud’s shape is a stable property of the population. Section 7.3 demonstrated exactly this on the descriptor data — high stability with low silhouette. Stability rules out partitions that are artefacts of one particular sample; it does not establish separation.

  1. Why did clustering the MD frames recover the six runs instead of conformational states, and what would you change?

Each run relaxed from the same starting structure into its own region of shape space and stayed there, and consecutive frames are strongly autocorrelated. The ARI against run identity was 0.503, against temperature 0.058, and three of the six runs occupied a single cluster each for the whole nanosecond. The fixes: microsecond trajectories, more replicas, a longer discarded equilibration, and clustering in a kinetically meaningful space (time-lagged independent components) rather than raw coordinates.

  1. How would you choose the Butina cutoff for (a) buying one analogue per series and (b) building a leave-cluster-out validation split?

  1. A tight cutoff (0.25–0.35) defines “the same chemical idea” narrowly, so one purchase per cluster still covers distinct ideas — at t = 0.35 the table gives 961 clusters. (b) A looser cutoff (0.4–0.6) produces fewer, broader clusters (344 at t = 0.6), which makes the training and test sides of the split genuinely dissimilar and the estimate appropriately pessimistic; with a tight cutoff, near-neighbours of a test compound remain in training and the split is only nominally cluster-based.

  1. Give the two statistics that should accompany any claim that a selected subset is diverse.

The mean pairwise distance within the subset and the minimum pairwise distance, each compared with the distribution obtained from many random subsets of the same size. Section 9 found the MaxMin pick 8.4 standard deviations above the random mean with no random set of 200 reaching it; the minimum distance separated the two strategies far more sharply (0.839 against an average of 0.211) than the mean did (0.905 against 0.842).

  1. Why is Davies-Bouldin inappropriate for comparing a DBSCAN result with a k-means result?

Davies-Bouldin measures the ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance, which assumes clusters are compact around a centroid. A crescent-shaped DBSCAN cluster has a large scatter about its centroid — which may not even lie inside the cluster — so the index penalises it regardless of how well it matches the data’s geometry. Internal indices are only comparable between methods that share a notion of cluster shape; otherwise compare on an external label or on a downstream task.

  1. A manuscript shows a UMAP of 5,000 compounds with eight visually distinct islands and concludes “eight chemotypes”. What do you ask for?

A clustering performed in the original fingerprint space with a stated metric and algorithm; the silhouette of that partition computed in that space; the sensitivity of the picture to perplexity and seed; and a negative control. Figure 14 showed four convincing islands in 50-dimensional Gaussian noise at every perplexity tried.

  1. When is it correct to say “no clusters were found”?

When the evidence says so: no knee in the k-distance curve, no plateau in the eps sweep, no valleys in the OPTICS profile, a gap statistic indistinguishable from its null, low silhouettes at every K and no agreement with any external label — all of which hold for the ROCK1 descriptor space. That sentence is publishable: it tells the next student not to repeat the analysis.

  1. You must deliver “one representative conformation per state” to a colleague for docking. What do you hand over and why not the centroid?

The medoid: the real frame whose RMSD to the cluster centroid is smallest, with its run, time stamp, cluster population and the cluster’s mean RMSD to its centroid (0.057–0.088 nm here). An average of coordinates distorts bond lengths and can collapse side chains, so it cannot be docked or deposited.

Glossary

Adjusted Rand index (ARI)
Agreement between two partitions corrected for chance: 0 for random agreement, 1 for identity.
Butina (leader) clustering
Single-pass clustering in which molecules sorted by neighbour count become cluster leaders and claim all unclaimed neighbours within a distance cutoff.
Centroid / medoid
The mean of a cluster’s members (may not be a real object) / the member closest to that mean (always a real object).
Cophenetic correlation
Correlation between original distances and the dendrogram heights at which pairs merge.
Core distance / reachability
In OPTICS, the distance to a point’s minPts-th neighbour, and the larger of that and the actual distance from the point being expanded.
Davies-Bouldin index
Mean over clusters of the worst ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance; lower is better.
DBSCAN
Density-based clustering with a radius and a minimum-point count; produces arbitrary shapes and explicit noise labels.
Elbow heuristic
Choosing K where the inertia curve stops falling steeply; it has no null model and bends even for structureless data.
Gap statistic
Difference between the expected log inertia of uniform reference data and the observed log inertia; zero means no more structure than noise.
Gaussian mixture model
Generative model of the data as a weighted sum of multivariate normals, fitted by expectation-maximisation, giving soft cluster memberships.
HDBSCAN
Hierarchical extension of DBSCAN that extracts the clusters most persistent across density levels, allowing clusters of different density.
Inertia
Within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids; the k-means objective, monotone decreasing in K.
Linkage
Rule defining the distance between two clusters in agglomerative clustering (single, complete, average, Ward).
Metastable conformation
A region of conformational space a molecule lingers in, relative to the time needed to cross between regions.
Responsibility
In a mixture model, the posterior probability that a given component generated a given observation.
RMSD
Root-mean-square deviation between two superposed structures; a Euclidean distance normalised by the number of atoms.
Silhouette
Per-object index comparing its mean distance to its own cluster with that to the nearest other cluster; ranges from -1 to 1.
Sparse matrix
Storage format that keeps only the non-zero entries; Matrix::sparseMatrix holds the 2,764 x 2,048 fingerprint matrix in the space of its 145,000 set bits.
Stability (of a clustering)
Agreement, measured by ARI, between partitions obtained from independent resamples of the same data.
Tanimoto (Jaccard) coefficient
Shared bits divided by the union of set bits of two binary fingerprints; ignores bits absent from both.
t-SNE / UMAP
Non-linear embeddings that preserve local neighbourhoods for visualisation; distances and apparent clusters in the map are not quantitatively interpretable.
Ward linkage
Agglomerative rule that merges the pair of clusters causing the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squares; in R, ward.D2 for distance input.
